extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners preparing/responding to Office actions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claims under the eligibility framework (Steps 1, 2A, 2B) including how to treat nature-based products, abstract ideas, laws of nature, and whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more.' Uses life-science and other examples to illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a new use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a step/act (process), machine, composition, etc., answer YES for Step 1 and proceed to determine whether the claim is directed to any judicial exception. Example uses: identifying that a claim reciting mixing and heating steps is a process; a Fourdrinier arrangement is a machine/combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is directed to an exception, continue through the 2A/2B evaluation. If not directed to any exception, the claim is eligible and further 2A/2B analysis is unnecessary. Examples: comparing sequences can be an abstract idea; using gravity per se is a law of nature but a machine that meaningfully limits its use may not be 'directed to' the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / nature-based product: compare to closest naturally occurring counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based product claims, compare the claimed nature-based product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if it has markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate disclosed altered properties (e.g., specific particle size distribution -> increased/consistent dissolution) to see if they yield a marked difference relevant to the invention. If the claimed product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart (and those differences are relevant to the claimed invention), it is not a ‘product of nature’ exception and may be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claimed nature-based product exhibits changed properties/characteristics that are a marked difference from the natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the altered property is relevant to the nature of the invention (e.g., release of sweetness over time). Use examples (Roslin) to contrast when claimed subject lacks markedly different characteristics. If marked differences exist, treat claim as not directed to 'product of nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — is the claim 'directed to' the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim, as a whole, is directed to the exception (for example, an abstract idea) or whether the additional elements remove it from being 'directed to' the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole is not directed to an exception, conclude eligibility at Step 2A and do not perform Step 2B. If it is directed to an exception, proceed to Step 2B (significantly more). Examples: certain hybridizing/detecting process claims are not directed to an exception and so are eligible at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — do additional elements amount to 'significantly more'?
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to an exception, determine whether any additional element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional elements that are merely instructions to apply the abstract idea using well-understood, routine, conventional techniques do not confer eligibility (Alice). However, recitation of unconventional, non-routine, specific techniques (or a meaningful combination of elements that together improve technology) can provide 'significantly more' (BASCOM, examples like SNOM or Cool-Melt PCR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate conventionality of additional elements at time of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether recited techniques/elements were well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field at the time the invention was made and the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of whether a technique was commonly used in the field at filing time controls: use by only a few scientists does not make a technique routine/conventional; widespread inclusion in lab manuals later does not retroactively make it conventional at filing time. Examples: SNOM or Cool-Melt PCR used by few scientists could be non-routine and thus supportive of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/tangible element recitation is insufficient by itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere recitation of a physical or tangible element (e.g., hybridizing step, sequencing step, machine parts) does not automatically confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A physical element that is recited at a high level of generality and reflects well-understood routine activity will not amount to significantly more. Examiner should explain why such elements are routine/conventional if relying on that conclusion (Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank).

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim focuses on a process, no need for product marked-difference analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If analysis of the claim as a whole shows the claim is focused on a process rather than on recited nature-based products, examiners need not perform the markedly different characteristics analysis on the recited product limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim directed to comparing sequences (a process) does not require performing the product-of-nature marked-differences test on recited genes/probes because the claim focus is the comparison process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental steps / human-performable steps indicate abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed steps could be performed by a human using mental steps or basic critical thinking, courts have treated such claims as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether steps like 'comparing information' are recited at high-level generality with no limits on how the comparison is performed. If so, they likely reflect an abstract idea (Classen, Myriad, Ambry examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of elements may yield significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements do not amount to significantly more, a specific combination of elements together may provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the claim as a whole — e.g., hybridizing + detecting by non-routine technique (SNOM) or comparing + Cool-Melt PCR amplification + sequencing can together be 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self-evident (claim as a whole clearly amounts to significantly more or clearly is not directed to an exception), a streamlined analysis may be appropriate and will not result in a written rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases, examiners need not perform the full Step 2A/2B analysis; nevertheless, remarks could be added to an Office action or reasons for allowance to clarify the basis (e.g., Fourdrinier machine that adds meaningful limitations and improves technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection drafting: identify the exception and explain insufficiency of claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection, identify the judicial exception the claim is directed to and explain why the claim elements amount to that exception and why additional elements/wherein clauses do not impose meaningful limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically point to the claimed comparison/abstract idea and explain why limiting language (e.g., a wherein clause) merely states a result and does not impose additional limiting steps. Explain absence of additional meaningful limitations in the claim as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance/remarks drafting for eligible claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim is eligible (either not directed to an exception or amounts to significantly more), examiners may add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance indicating that the claim is not directed to any judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use remarks to clarify that the claim recites additional limitations that, alone or in combination, are more than a mere instruction to apply the exception using well-understood, routine, conventional techniques, or that the claim adds meaningful limitations/improvements to technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting laws of nature may still be eligible if they add specific unconventional steps that effect transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim founded on a scientific/chemical principle or law of nature can be eligible if the claim does not recite the law and instead recites specific, unconventional steps that effect a transformation (e.g., hydrolysis process mixing/heating under specific conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim's specific steps effect a transformation (e.g., fat + water heated under pressure to produce free fatty acids and glycerol) and add meaningful limitations beyond the law itself; eligibility can be self-evident without full 2A/2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-of-filing field-level routine/conventionality assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining if a recited technique is well-understood, routine, and conventional, the relevant frame is the state of the art at the time the invention was made and the application filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let later widespread adoption (e.g., later inclusion in lab manuals) retroactively render a technique conventional at the earlier filing date. Consider contemporaneous literature and common practice among practitioners at filing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case law as analytical touchstones
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply relevant judicial decisions (e.g., Myriad, Mayo, Alice, Roslin, Diamond v. Diehr, Eibel Process Co., Tilghman) as precedential or illustrative guidance when identifying exceptions and evaluating whether additional elements are conventional or sufficient to confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases where applicable to explain why an activity is an abstract idea or why particular limitations do/don't amount to significantly more. Use examples from those cases to illustrate outcomes (e.g., Myriad: comparison/sequence claims; Diehr/Eibel: processes/machines that improve technology).
